source.title: Whitening and Second Order Optimization Both Make Information in the Dataset Unusable During Training, and Can Reduce or Prevent Generalization
source.authors: Neha S. Wadia; Daniel Duckworth; S. Schoenholz; Ethan Dyer; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper body, appendices, and references; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports training-accuracy or training-error stopping outcomes for CIFAR-10 models under different whitening and optimization conditions. These results bear on whether the tested models reach near-zero training error, although the paper's main question is generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports MLPs trained to 0.999 training accuracy and WRNs trained until training error was below 10^-3. CNNs were trained until 100% training accuracy. It does not report corrupted-label or random-label training results. Epoch and training-trajectory comparisons appear in figures; their exact values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The convolutional networks trained with full-batch gradient descent reach near-zero CIFAR-10 training error from random initialization, bearing on V1 through a different optimization recipe. The whitening and second-order optimization comparisons do not test V2–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors argue that whitening and certain second-order optimizers remove access to input information useful for generalization. Their experiments show faster training alongside worse generalization, while appropriately regularized second-order optimization can accelerate training and sometimes improve test loss.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies whitening and second-order optimization effects on generalization and convergence; it is not a direct reproduction of the claim's cited training-error studies. Its CIFAR-10 training outcomes use specified accuracy/error stopping criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: For CIFAR-10 MLPs, the epoch difference between unwhitened and train-whitened data varies with dataset size; the text identifies sizes below 50 as an exception. Whitening condition also changes reported generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 MLPs reach 0.999 training accuracy; whitening usually reduces epochs to that endpoint, with an exception below dataset size 50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input whitening can accelerate fully connected network training, with effects depending on dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: Unregularized Gauss-Newton reaches 100% CNN training accuracy and achieves its best validation loss about two orders of magnitude earlier than gradient descent, while generalizing worse. Regularization can preserve acceleration and improve test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Second-order preconditioning can accelerate training while changing generalization, with the tradeoff depending on regularization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 139 (2021)
record.problems: The training-error values for the MLP and CNN are reported as stopping criteria rather than as per-condition achieved outcomes. The MLP epoch comparison is plotted without exact values in the text. The Wide ResNet results use two random seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. The paper's test-error and test-loss results do not measure training classification error. The regularized Gauss-Newton experiment does not state a training-accuracy stopping criterion, so it is retained only as an indeterminate row (R7).

untested.parts: CIFAR-100; corrupted or random labels; SGD or Adam training of convolutional networks; systematic size comparisons; substantial training error under smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-minimum frequencies, and extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation and matched comparisons with identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Initialization comparisons measuring training speed, signal propagation, or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to an initial stability limit, catapult recovery, and sharpness evolution.
Matched batch-normalization comparisons and normalization-free Fixup training.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed V1 limits_scope verdict for very small MLP datasets: it concerns whitening's speed advantage, outside V1's architectural and outcome scope. Training endpoints are supported by explicit descriptions of completed training, but the paper does not provide separate final training-error measurements for every configuration.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, Adam, or comparisons with smaller models and early stopping. Its reported CIFAR-10 training outcomes use specified stopping thresholds; they do not establish behavior across the full range of sizes and recipes in the version.
